_note: Primary dataset: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) Master Catalog, the dataset listed on the Space Apps 2026 'Abandoned but not Forgotten' Resources page. nssdcId = the NSSDCA spacecraft record each object's dates, site, coordinates and fate come from. Story chapters: purpose = Designed, story = Mission, science = Discovery, fate = Left behind, legacy + status = Legacy. events = dated mission journey (YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD). thenNow = a later NASA orbital photo of the same hardware, used only where NASA's own description confirms what it shows. Coordinates: planetocentric degrees, east longitude positive (-180 to 180), converted from NSSDCA values. null = no verified value. statusType: 'in-use' or 'inactive'. Every fact is referenced in docs/research-sources.md

objects.name: Surveyor 3
objects.status: Inactive since May 1967. Apollo 12 took its camera and some parts back to Earth; the rest is still on the Moon.
objects.site: Oceanus Procellarum (Ocean of Storms), inside a 200 m crater
objects.purpose: A robotic lander sent to prove a spacecraft could land softly on the Moon and to study the surface, to prepare for crewed Apollo landings.
objects.story: Its engines kept firing, so Surveyor 3 touched down three times before settling inside a small crater on 20 April 1967. It sent back 6,326 TV pictures and used its scoop to dig trenches up to 18 cm deep.
objects.science: By digging and photographing, Surveyor 3 tested how firm the lunar soil was, information NASA needed to check that the Apollo design suited the lunar surface. Engineers and scientists later studied its returned parts to see what 31 months on the Moon had done to them.
objects.fate: It stopped working after sunset on 3 May 1967. On 19 November 1969, Apollo 12 landed about 180 m away. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over, and Conrad used cutters to remove its camera, scoop and other parts to bring back to Earth. The rest of Surveyor 3 is still in its crater.
objects.legacy: Apollo 12 made a "pinpoint landing" within walking distance of Surveyor 3, so astronauts could visit a robot that had landed two and a half years earlier and bring part of it home.

heritage.verified: NASA's 2011 guidance for future Moon missions names Surveyor among the U.S. heritage lander sites, and recommends that landers not fly over such sites within 2.0 km. It also notes that parts returned from Surveyor 3 showed chemical contamination from Apollo 12's rocket exhaust.

source.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), pp. 7 and 9

heritage.interpretation: Surveyor 3 is a scientific time capsule. It shows what years on the Moon do to a machine, and also how easily a visit can change the very thing being studied.

events.label: Bounces three times and lands in a crater
Astronauts remove its camera and parts

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 12 photo AS12-48-7134 (Alan Bean at Surveyor 3, Apollo 12 lunar module behind)

objects.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle (descent stage)
objects.status: Left on the Moon in July 1969, after serving as the launch pad for the crew's ascent stage.
objects.site: Tranquility Base, Mare Tranquillitatis (Sea of Tranquility)
objects.purpose: The bottom half of the lunar module. It held the landing rocket, fuel tanks, water, oxygen and storage for the science experiments, and carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin down to the surface.
objects.story: Eagle landed on 20 July 1969 at 20:17:40 UT, and Armstrong radioed: "Houston, Tranquility Base here - the Eagle has landed". A few hours later, at 02:56 UT on 21 July, Armstrong climbed down its ladder and stepped onto the Moon.
objects.science: Eagle was the first crewed vehicle to land on the Moon. It carried the first science experiments that astronauts set up on the lunar surface, including the laser reflector and seismometer in this collection.
objects.fate: When the moonwalk was over, the top half of the lunar module (the ascent stage) blasted off, using the bottom half as its launch pad, and carried the astronauts back to the command module. The descent stage stayed behind at Tranquility Base.
objects.legacy: A plaque on its ladder strut reads: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot on the Moon July 1969, A.D." Forty years later, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the landing site from orbit.

heritage.verified: NASA's 2011 guidance calls Apollo 11 "a watershed in human history and humanity" and recommends treating its site as unique: no visits to any part of it, and an exclusion zone of 75 m around the descent stage.

source.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

heritage.interpretation: Eagle's descent stage marks the first place people set foot on another world. Its value comes from being left exactly as the crew left it.

events.label: Armstrong steps onto the Moon, 02:56 UT
Ascent stage lifts off; descent stage stays
Landing site photographed by NASA's LRO

thenNow.caption: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter passed over the Apollo 11 landing site again in 2009, giving a new view of the historic site from orbit.

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 11 photo AS11-40-5903 (Buzz Aldrin beside a leg of Eagle)

objects.name: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
objects.status: Still used by scientists today. It is a passive mirror and needs no power.
objects.site: Tranquility Base, Mare Tranquillitatis (Sea of Tranquility)
objects.purpose: A 46 cm square panel of 100 special mirrors (corner cubes) that bounce laser light straight back to where it came from, so scientists on Earth can measure the exact distance to the Moon.
objects.story: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set it up near Eagle during their moonwalk in July 1969. Observatories on Earth fire laser pulses at it and time how long the light takes to come back.
objects.science: Laser ranging can measure the Earth-Moon distance to within a few millimetres. It showed that the Moon is slowly moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm every year, and it helps spacecraft that orbit and land on the Moon know exactly where they are.
objects.fate: The crew left it at Tranquility Base when they flew home in July 1969. Unlike the other experiments, it has no power to run out, so it was never switched off.
objects.legacy: The only object in this museum that is still used for science. Lunar laser ranging has provided data continuously for more than 57 years.

heritage.verified: NASA's 2011 guidance notes that the Apollo 11 reflector "continues to be an active scientific experiment" and recommends that laser ranging retro-reflectors "should be carefully preserved."

source.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), pp. 18 and 20

heritage.interpretation: Here heritage and science overlap: protecting this historic site also protects research that is still happening.

events.label: Still used: 57+ years of laser ranging

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 11 photo AS11-37-5551 (laser reflector in front, seismometer behind)

objects.name: Apollo 11 Passive Seismometer (EASEP)
objects.status: Inactive since August 1969, when it stopped responding to commands from Earth. Still on the Moon.
objects.site: Tranquility Base, about 17 m south of Eagle
objects.purpose: A solar-powered station to measure moonquakes and learn about the Moon's crust and interior. It also carried a detector to measure how much dust settled on it.
objects.story: Buzz Aldrin carried it out and set it up about 17 m south of the lander. It was switched on from Earth on 21 July 1969 while the astronauts were still outside.
objects.science: It was designed to measure seismic activity and the physical properties of the lunar crust and interior. Because it ran on solar panels, it could only work during the lunar day.
objects.fate: It got 30 °C hotter than planned but kept working, and it was switched on again for a second lunar day. On 27 August 1969 it stopped accepting commands from Earth, and the experiment ended. It is still on the Moon.
objects.legacy: Short-lived, but it worked: it was switched on from Earth while the astronauts were still on the Moon, and it kept running in heat 30 °C beyond its planned maximum.

heritage.verified: It was set up about 17 m from the descent stage, inside the Apollo 11 site that NASA's 2011 guidance recommends should not be visited (exclusion zone: 75 m around the descent stage).

source.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

heritage.interpretation: Short-lived as it was, it belongs to the first set of science experiments that people set up by hand on another world.

events.label: Arrives on the Moon aboard Eagle

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 11 photo AS11-40-5942 (Buzz Aldrin carrying the experiments)

objects.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
objects.status: Parked on the Moon since the Apollo 15 crew left in 1971.
objects.site: Hadley-Apennine, at the foot of the Apennine mountains (Mare Imbrium region)
objects.purpose: A car carried on the lunar module, so astronauts could travel much farther from their lander than on foot.
objects.story: Apollo 15 landed on 30 July 1971 at the foot of the Apennine mountains. On 31 July, David Scott and James Irwin unloaded the rover and drove it. Over three moonwalks they used it to explore areas up to 5 km from the lander.
objects.science: With the rover's help, the crew covered 27.9 km on three moonwalks and collected 77.31 kg of rocks and soil for scientists on Earth.
objects.fate: Only the top part of the lander flew back to orbit, so when the crew left, the rover stayed behind at Hadley-Apennine.
objects.legacy: It was the first time a vehicle like this had been used on the Moon, and NASA reports that its performance on the lunar terrain was very successful.

heritage.verified: NASA's 2011 guidance states that "all the Apollo sites represent significant historical/heritage value in material culture" and recommends that landers not fly over Apollo sites within 2.0 km.

source.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), pp. 7 and 17

heritage.interpretation: The first vehicle of its kind driven on the Moon, parked where its crew left it, is a landmark in the history of exploration vehicles.

events.label: Rover unloaded and driven for the first time

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 15 photo AS15-86-11603 (James Irwin at the rover)

objects.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP)
objects.status: Inactive since 30 September 1977, when all Apollo science stations were shut down. Still on the Moon.
objects.site: Taurus mountains south of Littrow crater, on the rim of Mare Serenitatis
objects.purpose: A science station left on the Moon to keep sending measurements to Earth after the astronauts went home. It was powered by a SNAP-27 radioisotope generator, not solar panels.
objects.story: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, the crew of the last Apollo landing, set it up during their first moonwalk. It was switched on on 12 December 1972. On the same mission the crew set off explosive packages for a seismic experiment, and Schmitt, the first scientist-astronaut on the Moon, discovered a patch of orange soil.
objects.science: It sent data from the Moon for almost five years after the last astronauts went home.
objects.fate: The crew lifted off on 14 December 1972, leaving the station running. On 30 September 1977 it was shut down along with all the other Apollo science stations.
objects.legacy: Set up by the last people to walk on the Moon, it was one of the Apollo stations that NASA shut down together on 30 September 1977.

heritage.verified: NASA's 2011 guidance treats the Apollo 17 site, the last Apollo landing, as unique alongside Apollo 11: no visits, and an exclusion zone of 225 m around the descent stage.

source.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

heritage.interpretation: It is a monument to the last time people walked on the Moon, and a reminder that science stations can keep working after the people who built them have gone home.

events.label: Shut down with all Apollo stations

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 17 photo AS17-147-22548 (ALSEP in the background)

objects.name: Viking 1 Lander
objects.status: Inactive since 13 November 1982, when contact was lost. Still where it landed.
objects.purpose: Study the biology, chemistry, weather, quakes, magnetism and surface of Mars from the ground.
objects.story: Viking 1 touched down in Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 and started sending its first surface picture just 25 seconds after landing. Its instruments then studied martian soil, weather and air.
objects.science: It sent back the first pictures from the surface of the Red Planet and studied martian soil, weather and air for more than six years.
objects.fate: Its seismometer never unlocked, and a stuck pin on its sampler arm took 5 days to shake loose, but the lander kept working until 13 November 1982, when contact was lost.
objects.legacy: NASA calls it the first truly successful landing on Mars. NASA's later Mars missions continue building on what the Vikings began.

heritage.verified: NASA calls Viking 1 the first truly successful landing on Mars, and says later Mars missions continue building on what the Vikings began.
heritage.interpretation: As the first long-lasting outpost on the surface of Mars, its landing site is arguably one of the most historic places on the planet.
heritage.unknown: We found no NASA heritage-protection guidance for hardware on Mars in our sources. NASA's 2011 recommendations cover sites on the Moon.

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA00381, the first photograph taken on the surface of Mars

objects.name: Sojourner Rover
objects.status: Inactive since 27 September 1997, when contact was lost. Still on Mars.
objects.site: Ares Vallis, an ancient flood channel near Chryse Planitia
objects.purpose: The first rover on Mars: a small six-wheeled rover (63 cm long, 28 cm high) sent to show that landing on and driving across Mars could be done at low cost.
objects.story: Mars Pathfinder landed on 4 July 1997 inside giant airbags, bouncing about 15 times before it stopped. Sojourner rolled down a ramp onto Mars on 6 July and drove among the rocks, while the lander photographed it and relayed its data to Earth.
objects.science: Sojourner tested rocks and soil in Ares Vallis, one of the largest outflow channels on Mars. It was carved by a huge ancient flood, possibly as much water as all five Great Lakes.
objects.fate: The lander and rover worked until 27 September 1997, when communications were lost for unknown reasons.
objects.legacy: The first rover on Mars. NASA's mission goal, to show that a low-cost landing and rover could work on Mars, was met.

heritage.verified: NASA describes Sojourner as the first-ever robotic rover delivered to the Martian surface.
heritage.interpretation: Its small size is part of its story: a 63 cm rover opened the era of driving on Mars.
heritage.unknown: We found no NASA heritage-protection guidance for hardware on Mars in our sources. NASA's 2011 recommendations cover sites on the Moon.

events.label: Lands on airbags in Ares Vallis

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA04318, Sojourner near the "Rock Garden"

objects.name: Spirit Rover
objects.status: Inactive since its last transmission on 22 March 2010. Stuck in soft sand, still on Mars.
objects.purpose: A robot geologist sent to search rocks and soils for clues about past water and whether life could ever have existed on Mars.
objects.story: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004 and drove off its landing platform on 15 January. It kept exploring even after one of its six wheels stopped working.
objects.science: Spirit travelled 7.73 km over 6 years and 2 months. It explored Gusev Crater, which may once have been filled with water.
objects.fate: On 23 April 2009 it broke through a thin crust into soft sand and got stuck. Its solar panels could not get enough sunlight to survive the winter, and its last transmission came on 22 March 2010.
objects.legacy: It kept exploring on five working wheels, and even after it got stuck it went on transmitting until March 2010.

heritage.verified: Spirit explored Gusev Crater for 6 years and 2 months, travelling 7.73 km, before its last transmission on 22 March 2010.
heritage.interpretation: Its final resting place, stuck in soft sand, is itself part of the record of how robots and Mars interact.
heritage.unknown: We found no NASA heritage-protection guidance for hardware on Mars in our sources. NASA's 2011 recommendations cover sites on the Moon.

events.label: Breaks into soft sand and gets stuck

objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA16442, Spirit self-portrait from the McMurdo panorama (2006)

objects.name: Opportunity Rover
objects.status: Inactive since 10 June 2018, when a planet-wide dust storm covered its solar panels. Still on Mars.
objects.purpose: Spirit's twin: a robot geologist looking for clues about past water and whether life could ever have existed on Mars.
objects.story: Opportunity arrived on 25 January 2004 and rolled to a stop inside a crater only 20 m wide. It kept exploring Meridiani Planum for more than 14 years.
objects.science: It explored Terra Meridiani, nicknamed the "Hematite Site" because it contains hematite, an iron-rich mineral that usually forms in water.
objects.fate: On 10 June 2018, as a planet-wide dust storm blanketed the solar-powered rover, it sent its last message to Earth. When the storm cleared, an orbiting camera could still spot it as a tiny blip.
objects.legacy: Opportunity drove 45.16 km, the longest drive on another world until NASA's Perseverance rover passed it on 11 October 2026.

heritage.verified: NASA reports that Opportunity's 45.16 km drive was the longest on another world until Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026.
heritage.interpretation: Its silent body marks the end of a 14-year journey, a record of how far a human-made explorer could travel on another world.
heritage.unknown: We found no NASA heritage-protection guidance for hardware on Mars in our sources. NASA's 2011 recommendations cover sites on the Moon.

events.label: Last message, during a dust storm
Seen from orbit after the storm
Its driving record is passed by Perseverance

thenNow.credit: NASA/JPL – PIA22549, "Opportunity After the Dust Storm" (2018)
thenNow.caption: On 20 September 2018, after the dust storm had cleared, the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed Opportunity from about 268 km up. The rover appears as a blip.

objects.name: Phoenix Mars Lander
objects.status: Inactive since 2 November 2008, when its solar power ran out at the end of summer. Still on Mars.
objects.site: Northern polar plains of Mars, about 68° N
objects.purpose: Dig into the icy ground of the Mars arctic to study water, ice and the polar climate, and whether the area could ever have supported life.
objects.story: Phoenix landed on 25 May 2008 in the far north of Mars, where the ground holds a lot of ice. Its robotic arm dug trenches and scooped soil into instruments on its deck.
objects.science: On 31 July 2008 NASA announced that Phoenix's instruments had identified water in a soil sample by heating it. Scientists called it the first time martian water had been "touched and tasted".
objects.fate: As the martian summer ended there was less sunlight for its solar panels, and it sent its last signal on 2 November 2008.
objects.legacy: Photos from orbit taken nearly a decade apart show dust slowly hiding the lander and the marks its landing left on the ground.

heritage.verified: NASA's 2008 announcement called Phoenix's result the first time Martian water had been "touched and tasted". Orbital photos from 2008 and 2017 show dust slowly covering the landing site.

source.name: NASA press release (31 Jul 2008) and NASA image PIA22223

heritage.interpretation: Its slow disappearance under dust shows that Mars, too, is changing these sites over time.
heritage.unknown: We found no NASA heritage-protection guidance for hardware on Mars in our sources. NASA's 2011 recommendations cover sites on the Moon.

events.label: NASA announces water found in a soil sample
Photographed from orbit, covered in dust

thenNow.credit: NASA/JPL – PIA22223, "NASA's Phoenix Lander on Mars, Nearly a Decade Later"
thenNow.caption: HiRISE photos from 20 July 2008 and 21 December 2017 show the same area, about 300 m wide. By late 2017, dust had hidden much of what was visible two months after landing.

objects.name: InSight Lander
objects.status: Inactive since its last contact on 15 December 2022 (dust-covered solar panels). Mission declared over on 21 December 2022.
objects.purpose: Listen for marsquakes and measure heat and the planet's wobble to find out what Mars is like inside: its core, mantle and crust.
objects.story: InSight landed in western Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018. Its robotic arm placed a seismometer on the ground to listen for marsquakes.
objects.science: Its seismometer recorded 1,319 marsquakes. Using them, scientists found that the crust under InSight is about 25 to 40 km thick and that Mars has a molten core about 1,800 km in radius, bigger than expected.
objects.fate: Over four years, dust slowly covered its solar panels. It last talked to Earth on 15 December 2022, and after it missed two more calls, NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022.
objects.legacy: InSight gathered new information about all three of Mars' major layers: crust, mantle and core. Seen from orbit in 2024, it had taken on the same reddish-brown colour as the rest of Mars.

heritage.verified: NASA reports that InSight gathered new information about Mars' crust, mantle and core. A 2024 orbital photo shows the lander taking on the same reddish-brown colour as the planet.
heritage.interpretation: Some of what we know about the inside of Mars came from a lander that is now fading into its landscape.
heritage.unknown: We found no NASA heritage-protection guidance for hardware on Mars in our sources. NASA's 2011 recommendations cover sites on the Moon.

events.label: Photographed from orbit, dusty and red

thenNow.credit: NASA/JPL – PIA26515, "HiRISE Studies the Dust on InSight" (image taken 23 October 2024)
thenNow.caption: The HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter shows InSight taking on the same reddish-brown colour as the rest of Mars, while the dark patch scorched by its landing rockets fades away.
